title: What Really Improves Mathematical Reasoning: Structured Reasoning Signals Beyond Pure Code
claim: Removing one data domain from pretraining sharply hurts its own capability and trades off against other capability dimensions.
layout: 6 line-plot panels in 2x3 grid, shared legend, score vs tokens
description: A 2x3 grid of line charts. Each panel plots score (y-axis) against training tokens in billions (x-axis, 10 to 200). Panel titles are Average, General Knowledge, Programming Ability, Mathematical Ability, Comprehensive Reasoning, and Professional Knowledge. Each panel shows three marked curves: full data in blue, w/o code in orange, and w/o math in green. The legend sits at the lower right of each panel. The two most striking panels are Programming Ability, where the orange w/o-code curve is far below the other two, and Mathematical Ability, where the green w/o-math curve is far below. In General Knowledge, Comprehensive Reasoning and Average, the w/o-code curve sits at or above the full-data curve. Professional Knowledge shows all three curves overlapping. The eye goes first to the two panels with a large gap between curves.
caption: The impact of three data compositions on model performance across capability dimensions. Starting from the 10T-token corpus, we ablate either the code corpus (w/o code) or the math corpus (w/o math), and then evaluate the resulting models along five dimensions: general knowledge, coding ability, mathematical ability, comprehensive reasoning, and professional knowledge. The results suggest clear trade-offs under a fixed-token training budget: code data competes with knowledge-intensive tasks, especially mathematical reasoning, whereas math data competes with tasks requiring comprehensive cross-domain reasoning.
abstract: Code has become a standard component of modern foundation language model (LM) training, yet its role beyond programming remains unclear. We revisit the claim that code improves reasoning through controlled pretraining experiments on a 10T-token corpus with fine-grained domain separation. Our findings are threefold. First, when code is restricted to standalone executable programs and Code-NL data are controlled for, code substantially improves programming ability but does not act as a general reasoning enhancer; instead, it competes with knowledge-intensive tasks, especially complex mathematical reasoning. Second, the reasoning gains often attributed to code are better explained by cross-domain structured reasoning traces, such as code-text and math-text mixtures, rather than by executable code alone. Third, increasing the density of structured math-domain samples within a fixed math budget yields substantial gains on difficult mathematical reasoning while largely preserving programming performance, suggesting that cognitive scaffolds offer a targeted way to mitigate cross-domain trade-offs. Finally, routing analyses show that data-composition effects are reflected in expert-activation patterns, providing mechanism-level evidence for competitive and synergistic interactions across domains. Our results clarify which data characteristics transfer across capability dimensions and point to more precise data-centric optimization strategies.
